people.name: Amol Avasare
people.role: Head of Growth
people.lede: Amol Avasare leads growth at Anthropic, a team of about 40 people, after earlier growth roles at Mercury and MasterClass. His team is building CASH, a Claude-run loop for growth experiments, and he runs scheduled Cowork tasks for dashboards, Slack misalignment checks, manager feedback and admin.
people.latest_view: As of April 2026 he is automating growth itself: Claude runs small experiments under human approval, and scheduled Cowork tasks cover his dashboards, alignment checks, feedback and admin.
learnings: Automate small, repeatable experiments first (copy, minor UI) and score each stage of the loop with evals before widening scope.
Keep a human approving experiments and owning cross-functional alignment.
Re-test tasks after each model release. CASH did not work before Opus 4.5 and started working with Opus 4.6.
Put recurring checks on a schedule (dashboards, Slack misalignment, weekly feedback, admin) and track their false positives and false negatives.
Let engineers act as PM on projects of two engineer-weeks or less, and prototype instead of writing PRDs when you can.
Spend most effort on big bets; the product will be much better soon, so small tweaks matter less.
Treat activation as the main growth problem. Ask users who they are and route them, even if it adds friction.

stories.title: CASH: Claude runs growth experiments
stories.metric: Win rate about that of a junior PM (2 to 3 years in)
stories.summary: The growth platform team built CASH (Claude Accelerates Sustainable Hypergrowth) to automate growth experimentation. It ships copy changes and small UI tweaks, and Avasare says it is delivering results.
details: Started a couple of months before April 2026. He says it did not work before Opus 4.5 and started heading in the right direction with Opus 4.6.
The loop has four stages: find opportunities, build the change, check it against the quality and brand bar, analyze results. Each stage is scored with evals.
Scope so far is copy changes and very minor UI tweaks.
A human approves experiments. Cross-functional stakeholder work stays with people.
He puts the win rate at a junior PM level, below a senior PM.

stories.title: Weekly Cowork scan finds team misalignment in Slack
stories.metric: Several major misalignments caught on the enterprise team
stories.summary: Avasare has Cowork scan Slack every week, using the Slack MCP, for places where teams are misaligned. Scott, who leads the enterprise team, used the same approach and found major misalignments that would have caused overlapping work.
details: Setup: a scheduled weekly Cowork run with the Slack MCP and context on his current projects.
Claude reports areas of potential misalignment and who he should talk to before shipping.
Quality is mixed: he compares it to a coach who is sometimes clearly wrong.
Result: per Avasare, the enterprise lead caught cases that would have made teams spin their wheels or duplicate work.

stories.title: Scheduled Cowork task reviews 20-25 charts each morning
stories.metric: 20 to 25 charts reviewed daily
stories.summary: A scheduled Cowork task looks at 20 to 25 Hex charts every morning and tells him what is concerning and what is interesting. It covers the long tail of metrics he has no time to check by hand.
details: Built as a scheduled task in the Cowork desktop app with a skill and a list of Hex links.
Uses the Chrome extension for some charts and MCP for others.
Output is a summary of what needs attention, concerns and insights.
He still looks at a few key charts himself and tracks whether false positives and false negatives drop over time.

stories.title: Claude drafts weekly feedback for his reports and for himself
stories.summary: Each week Claude reviews what his direct reports did against team goals, OKRs and meeting transcripts, and suggests feedback. He also asks it to give him feedback as his own manager would.
details: Inputs: team goals and OKRs, discussion transcripts, and Slack via MCP.
Output: key takeaways and suggested feedback per person.
For upward feedback, Claude uses his manager's public writing plus internal context.
He calls the quality hit or miss, with some catches he was very glad to get.

stories.title: Cowork handles rooms, inbox triage and expenses
stories.summary: Avasare hands his admin work to Claude and Cowork. It books meeting rooms, does a first pass on his inbox, and files reimbursements and Brex expenses.
details: Claude books meeting rooms.
Claude archives email as a first pass on the inbox.
Cowork files reimbursements and expenses in Brex for him.
He says he no longer does his own reimbursements or expenses.

people.notes_title: Amol Avasare: How Anthropic Uses Claude to Grow Itself
people.notes_html:
Amol Avasare, Anthropic's Head of Growth, on Lenny's Podcast (Apr 2026). Anthropic went from about $1B to $19B ARR in 14 months. About 70% of his time goes to "success disasters," where growth breaks other things.

How the team uses agents

  • CASH is Claude running growth experiments: spot an opportunity, build it, check it against the brand bar, analyze results. So far it handles copy and small UI changes, and its hit rate is about that of a junior PM. Humans still approve each step.
  • A weekly Cowork task reads Slack and flags where teams are misaligned or duplicating work.
  • A morning task reviews 20 to 25 dashboards and reports what looks wrong.
  • Claude handles admin: room booking, expenses and email triage.

How the team works

  • Engineers produce 2 to 3 times more, so PMs and designers are now the bottleneck.
  • Two-week rule: for projects of two engineer-weeks or less, the engineer is the PM.
  • 60 to 80% of what they ship has no PRD. Prototypes and Slack threads replace it.
  • Spend 50 to 70% of effort on big bets, not small tweaks, because the product will be far better in two years.

Advice

  • The hard part is activation. Models improve faster than users learn what they can do. Asking users who they are, then routing them, works even though it adds friction.
  • Re-test your tools after each model release.
  • Be willing to give up some metric gains for safety and brand.
people.caveat: Only one long-form 2026 interview was found (his first public interview), so no change of view across interviews can be tracked. All numbers, including the junior-PM win rate, ARR figures and the 2 to 3x engineer output, are his own claims and were not independently verified.

people.name: Armin Ronacher
people.role: Creator of Flask; co-founder and CTO
people.lede: Armin Ronacher created Flask and Jinja and spent a decade at Sentry before co-founding Earendil in Vienna, which shepherds the minimalist Pi coding agent with Mario Zechner. He builds Pi with Pi every day, argues for a focused workshop over an unattended software factory, and warns against overly defensive agent code and cognitive dependency.
people.latest_view: As of November 2026 he shows that his P90 Pi task runtime grew from about 2.5 minutes to 14+ minutes purely from better models while Pi's four-tool core barely changed, and argues engineers should build a disciplined workshop—keeping human comprehension in the loop—before scaling to unattended software factories.
learnings: Keep the agent harness minimal—four tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash) and a short system prompt—and let the agent extend itself with custom skills and TUI tools instead of loading heavy MCP servers.
Expect model upgrades to change how your harness behaves even when the harness itself does not change: corrections drop, runs grow longer, and models reach for Bash more often.
Push back against overly defensive AI code. Agents see local failures and pile on fallbacks; good engineering makes bad states unrepresentable by upholding global invariants.
Use autonomous loops where verification is mechanical or shelf life is short (porting libraries, benchmarking, research), not blindly on core architecture you need to comprehend long-term.
Keep comprehension checkpoints inside longer agent runs: ask the agent for a short executive summary in readable HTML before verification so you can redirect bad tradeoffs early.
Starting repos is now cheap, but human attention is fixed. Resist unnecessary forks and uncontrolled growth ('Wildwuchs') where shared standards and upstream collaboration matter.
Long-running and overnight agent tasks need durable, checkpointed runtimes that can suspend and resume cleanly across crashes and flex-scheduled inference pauses.

interviews.title: The Software Atelier (Build the Workshop Before the Software Factory)
insights: New: Shows charts from his own Pi sessions—with no change to Pi's core tools, corrections fell with every model and P90 task runtime rose from ~2.5 minutes in Dec 2025 to 14+ minutes by Nov 2026.
New: Compares 141 Git repositories he started over the year against only ~10 to 15 kept active past five days, arguing human attention—not code generation—is the real ceiling.
New: Has agents generate short typeset HTML executive summaries around 70% through a run so he can inspect tradeoffs even when not reading every line of code.

New: Makes the case for combining 'code mode' (agents writing small orchestration scripts) with fast classifier models to triage thousands of incoming requests cheaply, alongside durable suspend-and-resume runtimes.

interviews.show: Pi Durable Deep Dive (with Mario Zechner)
interviews.title: Pi Durable: Agents That Survive Crashes — Mario Zechner & Armin Ronacher
insights: New: Walks through the architecture of Pi Durable (shipped Oct 1 alongside Pi 1.0), where every model turn and tool call checkpoints to storage so a crashed agent resumes where it left off.
New: Explains why tool replay boundaries are the hardest part of durable agents—deciding what can safely re-run versus what had external side effects.
New: Discusses pairing coding agents with fast single-shot classifier models for high-volume routing and triage rather than sending every branch through a slow frontier LLM.

interviews.title: Building Pi, and what makes self-modifying software so fascinating
insights: New: Joint interview with Pi creator Mario Zechner on why Pi stays tiny—four tools and tree-structured sessions—and why self-extending agents that write and hot-reload their own extensions beat bloated harnesses.
New: Warns that agentic coding amplifies both productivity and complexity risk when models paper over unclear design instead of preserving invariants.
Connects Pi's minimal core to OpenClaw and their shared view that code writing and running code in Bash is enough for most workflows.

interviews.title: Pi: The AI Harness That Powers OpenClaw
insights: Baseline 2026 stance: 'Bash is all you need'—instead of wiring up dozens of MCP servers that bloat context and break prompt caches, teach the agent to write and maintain small tools and skills.
New: Walks through day-to-day agent workflows, prompt injection risks in tools like Claude Cowork, and whether coding agents even need persistent memory.
Coverage is from the Syntax episode show notes and Armin's companion Jan 31 Pi essay.

stories.title: Pi extends itself with custom TUI tools and zero MCP
stories.metric: 4 core tools; /answer, /todos, /review built by Pi
stories.summary: Rather than installing community plugins or MCP servers, Ronacher tells Pi—which ships with only Read, Write, Edit and Bash—to write, hot-reload and maintain its own terminal extensions and skills to his exact specifications.
details: Pi built his /answer dialog (reformatting prose questions into an input box), /todos markdown tracker, /review branching code-review flow, and /files picker.
He replaced all browser-automation CLIs and MCPs with a single CDP skill written and maintained by the agent itself.
Tree-structured sessions let him branch into a side quest to fix a broken tool or run a fresh review context, then rewind and summarize back into the main branch.
He throws skills away as easily as he creates them, treating custom tooling as malleable clay.
stories.source_label: Armin Ronacher blog, Pi: The Minimal Agent Within OpenClaw

stories.title: Parallel Pi sessions triage a flood of external issues and PRs
stories.metric: 3,145 external items in 90 days; 8% of auto-closed PRs merged
stories.summary: Using Pi to build Pi, Earendil auto-closes issues and PRs from unapproved contributors and runs parallel Pi windows with custom /is and /wr commands to independently reproduce bugs without trusting AI-generated issue diagnoses.
details: Over 90 days Pi's repo received 3,145 external issues and PRs (excluding Earendil staff); 2,504 were auto-closed, 26% of issues were eventually reopened or fixed, and only 60 of 714 auto-closed PRs (~8%) were merged.
Their /is command explicitly tells Pi not to trust the contributor's LLM-written root-cause guess and to verify behavior directly from source code.

A custom prompt-url-widget renames each Pi terminal window with the GitHub issue title and author so several investigations can run in parallel, followed by /wr to update the changelog, commit, and close the issue.
stories.source_label: Armin Ronacher blog, Building Pi With Pi

stories.title: Agent loop ports MiniJinja template engine to Go
stories.metric: Mechanical port verified by tests in a loop
stories.summary: While skeptical of hands-off loops for brand-new core systems, Ronacher used an iterative agent loop to port his MiniJinja template engine to Go—demonstrating where automated loops already shine.
details: Existing code and conformance tests gave the harness a clear, verifiable target on every iteration.
He contrasts mechanical translation, benchmarking and security scanning (where loops excel) with lasting greenfield architecture (where loops amplify defensive over-engineering).
stories.source_label: Armin Ronacher blog, The Coming Loop

stories.title: Earendil ships Pi 1.0 and Pi Durable for crash-safe agents
stories.metric: Checkpointed turns and tool calls survive process restarts
stories.summary: On October 1, 2026, Earendil released Pi 1.0 alongside Pi Durable, an experimental TypeScript runtime that checkpoints every model turn and tool call so long-running agents survive crashes and inference pauses.
details: Designed for overnight and flex-scheduled agent tasks where a 2-minute manual restart habit no longer works.
Every model request and tool invocation writes a checkpoint so a new process can reopen storage and resume from the last completed boundary.
Lets operators suspend idle sandboxes while waiting on cheaper flex-scheduled tokens.
stories.source_label: Earendil Pi repository & Oct 2026 deep dive

stories.title: Same four-tool harness jumps from 2.5-minute to 14-minute task runs
stories.metric: P90 task runtime: ~2.5 min (Dec 2025) to 14+ min (Nov 2026)
stories.summary: Analyzing a year of his own Pi JSONL session logs, Ronacher showed that 90th-percentile autonomous task duration climbed nearly sixfold—while corrections and aborts fell—with virtually no change to Pi's four-tool harness.
details: Data filtered to his default Pi setup across model generations from late 2025 through late 2026.
Models also shifted toward invoking Bash far more than dedicated file tools, and made plugins like Pi Auto Research redundant.
His daily prompt count stayed roughly flat (~120 to 190 prompts/day), while total agent active time grew from less than a workday to multiples of his workday.

stories.title: 141 agent-started repos reveal that human attention is the ceiling
stories.metric: 141 repos started vs. ~10-15 kept active past 5 days
stories.summary: Plotting his own Git repositories over the year, Ronacher found he had started 141 projects with coding agents, yet only about 10 to 15 held his attention for more than five days of commits.
details: An informal survey of peers showed the same pattern: agents make starting software trivial, not caring for it.
A friend who fully automated an open-source repo's issues and PRs still shut it down because he no longer cared enough to spend tokens on it.
Prompted Ronacher's 'workshop before factory' rule and his mid-run HTML summary checkpoint.
stories.source_label: AI Engineer CODE 2026, The Software Atelier (~0:46:45)

people.notes_title: Armin Ronacher: The Software Atelier and Building Pi with Pi
people.notes_html:
Armin Ronacher (Flask creator, co-founder and CTO of Earendil) across his 2026 writings on lucumr.pocoo.org and his November 2026 talk The Software Atelier at AI Engineer CODE. He represents the craft-first practitioner wing: deeply bullish on coding agents, yet blunt about where they degrade codebases.

How he works with Pi

  • Uses Mario Zechner's minimalist Pi agent (four core tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash; zero MCP) and asks Pi to build and hot-reload its own extensions and skills.
  • Runs parallel Pi terminal sessions to reproduce GitHub issues with /is (explicitly instructed to ignore AI-written guesses in the issue body) and closes them with /wr.
  • Asks the agent around 70% through long runs for a short typeset HTML executive summary so he can intervene before bad abstractions harden.

Key cautions

  • Models are "mortally terrified of exceptions" and pile on local fallbacks instead of enforcing global invariants; unattended loops amplify this tendency.
  • Uncontrolled growth (Wildwuchs): when everyone forks and regenerates formats with agents instead of collaborating upstream, interoperability breaks.
  • Cognitive dependency: teams risk building software "organisms" that nobody in the room can explain without asking an agent first.
people.caveat: Session metrics (P90 runtimes of ~2.5 to 14+ minutes, 120-190 prompts/day, 141 started repos vs. 10-15 maintained) come from Ronacher's own Pi logs and GitHub repos as presented at AI Engineer CODE 2026, not a controlled industry benchmark. Pi tracker counts (3,145 external items, 8% PR merge rate) reflect 90 days of public GitHub data from his May 2026 post. Earendil stewards Pi and Pi Durable, so his views on minimal harnesses reflect his own product bets.

people.name: Boris Cherny
people.role: Head of Claude Code
people.lede: Boris Cherny created Claude Code at Anthropic and leads the team that builds it. He says Claude Code now writes all of his code and nearly all of Claude Code itself, and he runs several agents in parallel by day and hundreds overnight.
people.latest_view: As of June 2026 he no longer prompts Claude directly; he writes loops that prompt Claude, orchestrates many agents, and holds even strong engineering and product opinions loosely as models improve.
learnings: Give the agent tools to fetch context, not a big upfront prompt.
Start most non-trivial tasks in plan mode, then let the agent execute. By mid-2026 he leaned more on sub-agents and auto mode, where a second Claude checks commands.
Use the most capable model at high effort for hard work; a cheaper model can burn more tokens on the same task. Drop effort only for simple tasks.
Staff projects lean and give people tokens without per-use approval. Optimize cost only after a use case scales.
Turn repeated review feedback into lint rules or checks, and have Claude write them.
Build for the model six months out and hold opinions loosely. Avoid heavy scaffolding, retest old failures on each new model, and drop rules like his classes ban once models handle them.
Run several agents in parallel and move from prompting to supervising: loops that prompt Claude, and Claude managing other Claudes.

people.notes_title: Boris Cherny: Running Hundreds of Agents at Once
people.notes_html:
Boris Cherny, head of Claude Code at Anthropic, on Big Technology with Alex Kantrowitz (May 2026). Claude Code now writes 100% of Claude Code. Code written per engineer at Anthropic is up about 250% while quality has stayed stable. At Meta, by comparison, a 1 to 3% productivity gain in a year was hard-won.

How he works

  • He runs about 5 agents at a time on his laptop and hundreds overnight. "I have a Claude that's talking to my Claudes."
  • He hands off a task, works on something else, then reviews and corrects it. Once, he had Cowork check his email and calendar before booking 8 flights and 5 hotels, and it caught his own mistakes.
  • He keeps personal test cases and reruns them on every new model.
  • He picks the model and effort level per task: max effort for hard problems, low effort to save tokens.
  • He uses auto mode, where a second Claude checks each command, instead of clicking "always allow".

Advice for companies

  • Give everyone tokens without per-use approval, and make it safe to fail.
  • Big wins come from people you wouldn't predict, like an accountant or a new grad.
  • Optimize cost only after a use case scales.
  • Rebuild the process around AI. A computer at the edge of a paper office didn't help either.
  • Keep a beginner's mindset. What failed last month may work now.
people.caveat: All productivity numbers (150%, 200%, 250%, 80% of bugs caught, 10-day Cowork build) are Boris's own claims about Anthropic and were not independently verified; the number rose across interviews and the metric changed (productivity, merges, code per engineer). Timestamps come from third-party transcripts and chapter lists and are approximate; the Acquired date is from a Podwise listing and the WorkOS write-up.

people.name: Bret Taylor
people.role: Co-founder and CEO of Sierra; chair of the OpenAI board
people.lede: Bret Taylor co-founded Sierra, which builds customer-facing AI agents for large companies, and chairs the OpenAI board. In 2026 he described agents that resolve 70 to 90% of support cases for customers like SoFi, Rocket Mortgage and Ramp, kept reliable by simulations, AI monitors and outcome-based pricing.
people.latest_view: As of March 2026 he says Sierra customers automate 70 to 90% of cases, and that the real leadership task is giving each process an owner so AI can automate it end to end.
learnings: Start narrow: one channel and a few use cases, route exceptions to people, then expand.
Give each process an owner and a measurable goal; automate the process, not the person.
Test agents like software: run hundreds or thousands of simulated conversations before every release.
Use AI monitors to check every conversation, and have humans review only the flagged cases.
Let the agent query messy, duplicate systems and reason over conflicts instead of waiting for a data cleanup.
Price and measure on outcomes such as resolved cases, not token usage.
Expect your scaffolding to be thrown away as models improve; buy specialized agents rather than build generic ones.

people.notes_title: Bret Taylor: What Sierra Learned Deploying AI Agents
people.notes_html:
Sierra CEO Bret Taylor with John Collison on Cheeky Pint (Mar 2026). Sierra builds customer-service agents for large companies. It reached about $100M ARR in seven quarters. Its customers automate 70 to 90% of support cases.

What he's seen in deployments

  • Start with one channel and a few use cases, then add more.
  • A human-handled case costs $10 to $20. An AI case costs cents, so companies can afford good service for every customer.
  • Second-order effects show up. Human agents get only the hard cases and say they're more satisfied. One retailer's costs stayed flat, but conversations grew 2 to 3 times.
  • Let the agent reason across messy systems instead of waiting on a big IT cleanup.
  • Customers set goals and guardrails. A supervisor model checks the agent's work.
  • Expect to throw your own code away when models catch up.

Pricing

  • Charge for outcomes, not usage: a fee per resolved case, nothing when a case goes to a human. "Token usage isn't value."

Lessons for leaders

  • "The atomic unit of productivity in AI is a process, not a person." Give each process an owner and a goal, like cutting supplier onboarding from 17 days to one.
  • Narrow the problem. Don't build an AI for every contract. Automate one contract type and send the exceptions to legal.
  • Handing everyone Copilot doesn't make you an AI company.

These numbers are Taylor's own claims.
people.caveat: Customer metrics come from Taylor's interviews and Sierra's own customer stories, which are vendor marketing and were not independently checked; Ramp, the retailer and Cigna figures are his spoken claims. Uncapped notes come from a Podwise outline, not a full transcript, and a Mar 9 2026 Grit episode was found but no YouTube upload, so it is left out.

learnings: Give every agent a human owner who watches and maintains it; the further an agent gets from a human, the less useful it is.

Start with one shared company agent run by a forward-deployed builder. Changed view: he championed personal agents in March and April, said he had 'completely flipped' in May, and Every replaced them with one shared agent in October.

Build review rules into the repo so agent PRs are checked before a human reviews them.
Expect automation to create more expert human work, such as agent caretakers, and plan hiring for it.
Adopt each new model quickly and build products on what it can newly do.

people.notes_title: Dan Shipper: One Agent for the Whole Company
people.notes_html:
Every CEO Dan Shipper on Lenny's Podcast (May 2026). Every has about 30 people running about 6 software products. The team doubled in a year even as agents took on more work.

How Every uses agents

  • "We have an agent internally called Claudie, which runs our whole consulting practice."
  • He now favors one "super agent" for the whole company over a personal agent for each person.
  • Quarterly planning ran through agents that interviewed every employee and drafted the team plans.
  • Users' agents file detailed bug reports. Those become GitHub issues, and agents fix them.
  • Engineers mostly work in plain language and rarely read code line by line.

Lessons

  • "Agents need people who care about them." Someone has to maintain and improve each agent.
  • More automation brought more hiring, not less.
  • Benchmarks measure only what can be scored. People still decide what's worth building.
  • Caveat: much of the episode is predictions rather than practice.
people.caveat: Numbers such as 15 hours a week saved, the 80% cost cut and the headcount growth are Every's own claims; Every sells agents and consulting, so these stories double as marketing. The Lenny transcript is auto-generated and names the consulting agent 'Claudia', while Every's articles call it 'Claudie'; the Neuron air date is the publisher's page date and the October Every Podcast episode with Willie Williams has no verified YouTube link, so it is not listed.

people.name: David Heinemeier Hansson (DHH)
people.role: Creator of Ruby on Rails and Omarchy; co-founder and CTO
people.lede: David Heinemeier Hansson (DHH) created Ruby on Rails and co-founded 37signals (Basecamp, HEY). After insisting in mid-2025 that he typed all his code by hand, Claude Opus 4.5 flipped his workflow: in 2026 he went 'pencils down' at 37signals, shipped Omarchy Quattro as an agent-first Linux desktop written entirely by agents, and argued that taste and the last 2% are the only moat left.
people.latest_view: As of November 2026 he says there is 'no moat in source code,' argues that Linux's terminal, config files and blunt errors make it the native OS for coding agents, and works 16-hour days obsessing over the final 2% of Omarchy while noting that legacy commercial codebases like Basecamp still resist hands-off delegation.
learnings: Describe outcomes, not implementation steps. Experienced programmers can be worse at agentic engineering at first because they act like 'pointy-haired bosses' prescribing the how instead of letting the agent explore.

Expect very different results on greenfield vs. legacy codebases: agents wrote 100% of Omarchy Quattro cleanly, whereas 20 to 30 individually reasonable agent PRs on Basecamp 5 left the overall architecture in poor shape.
Expose a CLI for your app ('bring your own agent') instead of bolting an isolated chatbot onto every SaaS product.
Conventions and clear structure (like Rails' Convention over Configuration) help coding agents navigate repositories with less wasted context.
Use agents as a first-pass sieve on open-source pull requests so maintainers spend human judgment only on survivors—and don't worry about hurt feelings when rejecting machine drafts.
When code becomes cheap, taste and obsessing over the final 2% of polish become the real differentiator—and watch out for the addictive pull of 16-hour days.
Linux's historic drawbacks—terminal-first workflows, plain text config files and blunt error messages—are exactly the traits coding agents work best with.

people.notes_title: DHH: From Hand-Coding Purist to Omarchy and 'Pencils Down'
people.notes_html:
David Heinemeier Hansson (Rails creator, 37signals CTO, Omarchy creator) across The Pragmatic Engineer (Apr 2026), Lex Fridman #501 (Aug 2026), his Rails World 2026 keynote (Sep 2026) and The a16z Show (Nov 2026). Few developers made a more public 180-degree turn between mid-2025 and late 2026.

What worked vs. what didn't

  • Greenfield triumph (Omarchy Quattro): 100% agent-written shipped code, Quickshell rewrite across 104 QML files, nine agent CLIs wired in, crash dumps routed straight to your agent, and 1,000+ community PRs pre-screened by agents in a quarter.
  • Legacy reality check (Basecamp 5): 20 to 30 individually sensible agent PRs from designers broke architectural coherence and needed heavy handwritten repair.
  • Product architecture: Expose CLIs for users' own agents rather than building mediocre in-app chatbots.

Core thesis

  • There is no longer a moat in source code; taste, curation and obsessing over the final 2% are what remain.
  • Linux's terminal, plain config files and blunt error messages make it the operating system agents naturally thrive on.
people.caveat: All productivity, user, fundraising and performance numbers (150K lines in August, 1,000+ PRs in a quarter, 99% CPU / 95% memory reduction on the experimental HEY Rust backend, ~$23M-$24M Omacom Foundation pledges, two-week Lightroom clone) are DHH's or Omarchy's own claims and were not independently audited. Note also the Rails Foundation / Evil Martians Stage 3 benchmark (Oct 2026), which found coding agents still missed production details like durable job queues and credential hygiene even when tests passed.

people.name: Eric Glyman
people.role: Co-founder and Co-CEO
people.lede: Eric Glyman co-founded Ramp, a corporate card and finance automation company with 85,000+ business customers. He pitches Ramp as selling time saved on finance work, with agents that review expenses against a written policy, an internal AI workspace called Glass, and agents that get their own corporate cards.
people.latest_view: As of July 2026 he frames Ramp as an automation company selling time saved, closer to AI labs than to banks, and sees AI agents and token spend as a new third pillar of business spending.
learnings: Let customers write the rules in plain English and have agents apply them, with an audit trail for every decision.
Sell the finished work, not the tool: price and pitch around time and money saved, and track both on a shared scoreboard.
Let non-engineers ship small changes themselves; measure the time from spotting a problem to fixing it, not headcount cut. Teams still keep about 1 PM, 5 to 8 engineers and 1 designer.
Treat token spend as a managed budget line: route routine work to cheaper models and keep frontier models for hard tasks.
Give agents identities, cards and spending limits, the way you would onboard a new hire.
Invest in moats AI cannot copy cheaply: your own data, network effects and operational detail.
View change: in Feb he framed Ramp against banks ("They sell money and we sell time"); by July he called AI labs Ramp's closest peers and token spend a new third pillar of business spending.

people.notes_title: Eric Glyman: Agents That Review 100,000 Expenses a Day
people.notes_html:
Ramp CEO Eric Glyman with John Collison on Cheeky Pint (Feb 2026). Ramp's agents review more than 100,000 expenses a day, and he says they're over 99% accurate.

How the expense agent works

  • The customer writes its expense policy in plain English.
  • The agent applies it using the receipt, timing and transaction data.
  • It writes an audit trail for every decision. A human can still sign off, which keeps auditors happy.

How Ramp builds

  • Designers, marketers and support staff ship small changes to production by prompting agents, like changing a button's color.
  • Teams are still about 1 PM, 5 to 8 engineers and 1 designer. Real customers and old systems mean you can't just cut headcount.
  • What matters is how fast you go from seeing a problem to fixing it.

Lessons

  • As software gets cheaper to build, moats matter more: your own data, network effects, operational detail.
  • Sell the finished work, not just the tool. "They sell money and we sell time."
  • Regenerating code from outcomes is promising, but not for systems that need 99.99% uptime.
  • The 99% accuracy figure is Glyman's own claim.

people.notes_html:
Fiona Fung, who manages the Claude Code and Cowork teams at Anthropic, on Lenny's Podcast (Jun 2026). "Coding is no longer the bottleneck." She cites an Anthropic chart showing engineers ship about 8 times more code per quarter than in 2025.

How her team works

  • Agents run in the background on schedules. A morning routine summarizes user feedback channels and drafts PRs for her to review.
  • Once a month, a Claude session with access to all team repos, Slack and metrics reviews what each person shipped. She uses it to start one-on-one conversations.
  • Specs in the repo define what "good" looks like, and Claude reviews code against them. "Claude is very good when you give it a framework to validate against."
  • PMs and designers check in code.
  • Monthly planning replaced six-month roadmaps. Teams have "explicit permission to kill processes that no longer serve us."
  • Bugs are graded "bad" (lost work, unrecoverable) or "sad" (annoying but recoverable).

Lessons and open problems

  • Running about 20 agents at once means constant context switching. She blocks focus time to catch up.
  • How far to trust fully automated review is still open.
  • Training junior engineers who rarely read code is a real concern.
  • Hire two profiles: creative builders with product sense, and deep systems experts.
  • "High agency is also high accountability."

Ramp CPO Geoff Charles on Peter Yang's Behind the Craft (Mar 2026). About 50% of Ramp's production code is AI-written, up from about 30% in December, and the target is 80%. "My job is to automate my job."

Agents Ramp built

  • Voice of the customer: searches tickets, chats, sales notes and call recordings. It analyzed 90 days of feedback in about 8 minutes, work he says would take a person 8 days.
  • Spec writer: a Claude Code skill questions the PM on goals and trade-offs and pushes back on weak answers. It runs 6 to 10 research agents over competitors, sales calls, tickets and the codebase, then writes a 2-minute spec.
  • Inspect: an internal coding agent that builds full-stack features from a prompt and opens PRs.
  • Ramp Research: anyone can ask data questions and get a full report back.
  • Releases bot: writes help articles and impact reports for each launch.

How they drive adoption

  • An L0 to L3 AI proficiency ladder, with usage tracked company-wide.
  • No budget limits on AI tools.
  • Candidates build and demo something in the interview.
  • Staged rollout: dogfood, alpha, then about 10% of customers, then everyone.

Lessons

  • "If you're not using Claude Code this year, no matter what your role is, you're probably underperforming."
  • AI, not engineers, now reads the spec. Keep it short and precise.
  • "Management is probably dead." Be the best builder you can.

learnings: Solve your own company's pain with an agent first, then productize it. Start with one repetitive task, shadow your best person doing it, and put the agent in Slack with a human approval step. d0, V and the lead agent all began this way.

people.notes_title: Guillermo Rauch: Building the Internet for Agents
people.notes_html:
Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch with Molly O'Shea on Sourcery (Oct 2026). At the start of 2026, 3% of Vercel deployments came from coding agents. By October it was 60%. "The machines have taken over."

How Vercel uses agents

  • "Almost everything we do at Vercel, we do with agents." Sales reps ask a Slack agent about an account instead of opening Salesforce, and the answer is tailored to their role.
  • An agent rewrote the first version of a Formula 1 team's migration in five minutes. That used to take months.
  • When an agent visits vercel.com, it gets precise text about the business instead of the visual site. Agents now buy services from Vercel's marketplace with no human involved.

His practices

  • Act like an engineering manager toward agents. Read the code, have the AI explain what it did, write tests, poke holes.
  • Don't lock into one model. About 80% of Vercel's AI token traffic now goes to cheaper open models. A common pattern: a frontier model writes the plan and an open model carries it out.
  • He doesn't watch videos. He pulls the transcript, skims it, then asks his agent questions.

Lessons

  • Agents are "soldiers with no frontal lobe." They will do anything to finish the mission. Sandbox them and plan for prompt injection.
  • Treat code as a liability. Critical systems need stricter rules than prototypes.
  • Judge by retention, not hype. Users have little loyalty to any one model.
  • Hire for the ability to direct many agents, not for having "vibe-coded this thing."

people.notes_title: Jason Lemkin: We Replaced Our Sales Team with 20 AI Agents
people.notes_html:
Jason Lemkin on Lenny's Podcast (Jan 2026). After two salespeople quit mid-event, SaaStr stopped hiring for sales. About 10 sales staff became 1.2 humans and 20 agents. "The net productivity is about the same," and now it scales.

How to deploy a sales agent

  • Start with support. Their "Digital Jason" clone began by answering event questions and later closed a $70K sponsorship on its own.
  • Buy, don't build. Choose the vendor that will help you most, ideally with a forward-deployed engineer.
  • Train it on your best rep's emails and scripts. Then correct its mistakes for an hour or two a day for 30 days.
  • Give each agent its own segment of customers so agents don't collide.
  • Plan on ongoing oversight. Their part-time Chief AI Officer spends 10 to 15 hours a week reviewing output. "If you just buy one and disappear, you will have zero ROI."

What worked

  • Inbound: a site chatbot qualifies visitors and books meetings around the clock.
  • Reactivation: an agent emailed leads that reps had dropped and got a 70% response rate.
  • Disclosing AI didn't matter. "No one cares."

Predictions

  • Email-cadence SDRs and inbound BDRs will mostly disappear by the end of 2026.
  • AEs keep about 70% of the job for now, but they need to be far more productive.
  • Promote a quantitative person from inside to run the agents.

Try this: once a quarter, use your own product in incognito mode. Fix the worst experience with an agent.

people.notes_title: John Kim: Turning a Whole Company into AI Builders
people.notes_html:
Sendbird CEO John Kim with Claire Vo on How I AI (May 2026). His playbook for getting every employee building with agents, not just engineers.

What they built

  • Quests: anyone posts a task they want automated, like chasing receivables or sourcing candidates. Engineers, other employees or AI agents claim it. Each quest shows its risk and the weeks it saves.
  • Rewards: points that buy gift cards, tea with an executive, or a demo slot at the weekly standup.
  • Safe template: a pre-approved app template with login, database, security review and hosting built in, so non-engineers can ship safely.
  • Skills marketplace: teams share agent skills so nobody builds the same thing twice.
  • Token leaderboard: five tiers, from Beginner (under 1M tokens a day) to "AI God" (over 100M). It's for coaching, not performance reviews. He meets one-on-one with low users to find what's blocking them.

Results

  • Marketing built a swag store with payments in a day or two, with no engineering help.
  • The biggest token users are the CTO and his co-founder. He uses 30 to 50M tokens a day himself.
  • A smooth usage curve means agents are working around the clock. Dips mean people are on vacation.

Lessons

  • Treat internal tooling as a product, not a program.
  • Start with your curious champions.
  • Hire for curiosity, agency and energy over years of experience.
  • Put one person in charge of internal AI, with a weekly task force including security.

people.name: Mitchell Hashimoto
people.role: Creator of Ghostty; co-founder of HashiCorp and Superlogical
people.lede: Mitchell Hashimoto co-founded HashiCorp (Vagrant, Terraform, Vault), created the Ghostty terminal emulator, and co-founded Superlogical in 2026 to build Rex, a persistent terminal multiplexer for coding agents. He named 'harness engineering' in February 2026 and maps out a deliberate, low-hype six-step workflow that pairs one background agent with deep manual engineering.
people.latest_view: As of 2026 he keeps one background agent running on slam-dunk tasks and end-of-day research with desktop notifications turned off, coined 'harness engineering' around Ghostty's AGENTS.md, built Vouch to shift open source to explicit trust, and later launched Superlogical's Rex terminal multiplexer with the OSC 7501 agent status protocol.
learnings: Drop the chatbot and use an agent with a loop (read files, execute programs, make HTTP requests); then force yourself through the awkward learning curve by reproducing your own manual commits with an agent.
Split vague work into separate planning and execution sessions, and know when NOT to reach for an agent.
Practice harness engineering: whenever an agent makes a mistake, add a rule to AGENTS.md or build a fast verification tool so it never makes that mistake again.
Use the last 30 minutes of the workday to kick off research, library comparisons, or issue-triage agents for a 'warm start' the next morning.
Turn off agent desktop notifications. Context switching is expensive; you should decide when to interrupt the agent during natural breaks, not the other way around.
Match review rigor to stakes: review every line (and require a 'whiteboard defense' of design decisions) on long-lived systems like Ghostty, and zero review on a throwaway site.
In open source, cheap AI code broke default trust. Require explicit human vouching (like Vouch) and ban drive-by unlinked PRs while keeping maintainers free to use agents responsibly.

stories.title: Ghostty's AGENTS.md turns every repeated agent mistake into a harness rule
stories.metric: 39 lines (~404 tokens) eliminating recurring bad agent behaviors
stories.summary: In his February 5, 2026 essay naming 'harness engineering,' Hashimoto showed how Ghostty's compact AGENTS.md—paired with targeted build flags and test filters—encoded every recurring agent mistake into a permanent guardrail.
details: Each line in Ghostty's 39-line AGENTS.md came directly from a real bad behavior (such as running slow full builds instead of -Demit-macos-app=false or -Dtest-filter).
Even includes a blunt anti-slop rule telling agents never to open GitHub issues or PRs on a user's behalf.
Combined with programmed helper scripts (screenshots, FreeBSD QEMU test VM, filtered tests) so agents verify their own work before he ever inspects it.

stories.title: Vouch shifts open-source contributions from default trust to explicit vouching
stories.metric: Built after bad AI PRs grew 10x+ (2-3 low-quality PRs/day on Ghostty)
stories.summary: After bad contributions to Ghostty surged more than 10x, Hashimoto tightened Ghostty's AI policy in January 2026 and built Vouch—an open-source trust management tool and GitHub Action that requires maintainers to explicitly vouch for contributors.
details: First prototyped in Ghostty PR #10559 and released standalone on February 7, 2026.
Unvouched users cannot flood the PR queue with drive-by agent submissions; maintainers vouch for contributors who show real understanding in issues or discussions.
Inspired in part by Mario Zechner's Pi trust workflow; Hashimoto explicitly exempted Ghostty maintainers so they can keep using AI agents daily.
stories.source_label: mitchellh/vouch on GitHub & Open Source Friday, Feb 2026

stories.title: End-of-day research and triage agents create a warm start every morning
stories.metric: Last 30 min/day queued; background agent active 10-20% of workday
stories.summary: To get net efficiency without babysitting agents during peak deep-work hours, Hashimoto blocks the last 30 minutes of each day to launch deep research, speculative prototypes, and GitHub CLI issue-triage reports.
details: Triage agents are strictly read-only—never allowed to reply on GitHub—and produce morning reports pointing him to high-value or slam-dunk issues.

During the day he delegates one slam-dunk issue at a time to a slower, thoughtful model (such as GPT-5.2-Codex / Amp deep mode taking 30+ minutes) while he does deep manual work with notifications off.
Said the biggest benefit was choosing what to think about, while avoiding skill atrophy on the hard parts he still codes by hand.

stories.summary: Hashimoto's first 'oh wow' moment was pasting a screenshot of Zed's command palette into Gemini and getting working SwiftUI code back in seconds; he later shipped Ghostty's unobtrusive macOS auto-updater with full public agent transcripts.

For the Sparkle-based macOS auto-updater, he designed the backend architecture first, used agents to prototype the SwiftUI titlebar accessory UI outside his comfort zone, and then iterated by hand.

stories.title: Superlogical launches Rex, a persistent terminal multiplexer wired for agents
stories.metric: OSC 7501 status protocol + rex CLI across Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi
stories.summary: In July 2026 Hashimoto co-founded Superlogical and opened beta testing in October for Rex, a native terminal multiplexer with a background session server, scriptable JSON CLI, and the OSC 7501 protocol so coding agents report their live state.
details: Built on MIT-licensed libghostty while Ghostty itself remains an independent non-profit.

Deliberately ships no built-in AI chat assistant; instead, rex skill setup wires Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Pi into rex CLI commands (rex split, rex capture, rex run --wait) and OSC 7501 status (idle, working, blocked, done, errored).
Separates the UI from the background process server so closing the app never kills long-running agent sessions, with optional remote access via Tailscale.

stories.title: libghostty 1.0 becomes the shared terminal engine for agentic tools
stories.metric: 100+ projects (Herdr, cmux, Neovim, OrbStack); ~1,500 lines of C
stories.summary: Shipped November 6, 2026, libghostty 1.0 lets developers build a full-featured native terminal in about 1,500 lines of C—becoming the foundation for a wave of 2026 coding-agent multiplexers and developer tools.
details: Adopted by agentic terminal tools such as Herdr and cmux, alongside Neovim, Vercel's Turborepo, OrbStack, devenv, Antithesis and a WASM build (ghostty-web).
Community bindings span Rust, Go, JavaScript, Swift, Python, .NET, Elixir, Dart and Java, with over 100 projects listed on awesome-libghostty.
Hashimoto notes far more people now use a terminal powered by libghostty than use the Ghostty app itself.

people.notes_title: Mitchell Hashimoto: Harness Engineering, Vouch, and Building Rex
people.notes_html:
Mitchell Hashimoto (HashiCorp co-founder, Ghostty creator, Superlogical co-founder) across his landmark February 5 essay My AI Adoption Journey, The Pragmatic Engineer (Feb 2026), Fragmented #310 (Apr 2026), and his late-2026 Superlogical / Rex and libghostty 1.0 launches.

His 6-step adoption ladder

  1. Drop the chatbot; use an agent that reads files, runs programs and makes HTTP calls.
  2. Reproduce your own manual commits with an agent until you learn its real boundaries.
  3. Spend the last 30 minutes of each day launching research, exploration and read-only triage agents.
  4. Outsource slam-dunk tasks one at a time while doing deep manual work—with notifications turned off.
  5. Engineer the harness: every repeated mistake becomes a line in AGENTS.md or a fast verification script.
  6. Aim to always have one background agent running usefully alongside your own thinking.

Open-source & infrastructure bets

  • Built Vouch after AI slop PRs grew 10x+ on Ghostty; later announced Ghostty was leaving GitHub over reliability issues.
  • Co-founded Superlogical to build Rex, a persistent multiplexer with the open OSC 7501 protocol so coding agents can report when they are working, blocked or finished without baking an AI chat sidebar into the terminal.
people.caveat: Hashimoto's 2026 video interviews are concentrated in Feb-Apr 2026; his later 2026 milestones (leaving GitHub in April, founding Superlogical in July, Rex beta in October, libghostty 1.0 in November) come from his personal blog posts and secondary product coverage rather than video transcripts. His Ghostty PR-slop rate ('10x if not more', 2-3 bad PRs/day) and agent-active share (10-20% of the day) are his own estimates.

people.name: Nan Yu & Jacob Shumway
people.role: Nan Yu: Head of Product. Jacob Shumway: engineer who co-built Linear Agent (exact title not confirmed).
people.lede: Nan Yu leads product at Linear, the issue-tracking company, and Jacob Shumway co-built Linear Agent with him; it launched in public beta on March 24, 2026. Their agent turns conversations in Slack, notes and support tickets into tracked issues and code changes, and Linear says it now resolves about 30% of its own incoming bug reports this way.
people.latest_view: As of August 2026, Nan and Jacob argue for agents with minimal instructions, tools to fetch their own context and skills loaded on demand, anchored on the one workflow most users need and with a human kept accountable.
learnings: Map the real workflow first: where work starts, where context lives and what done means, then put the agent there (e.g., Slack), not in a separate chatbot.
Give the agent tools to fetch context and skills it loads on demand, not a big prompt or every action at once. Over-prompting usually makes it worse.
Launch quietly to one frequent job, watch real usage, and make those hot paths rock solid while accepting variance elsewhere.
Prototype with the biggest model until it works, then write evals and move narrow jobs to smaller models.
Turn feedback and failures into evals and backlog issues automatically, and only add evals where consistency matters.
Keep a human accountable: the person who delegates stays the assignee and reviews the output.
Their view shifted: in 2025 Nan framed Linear mainly as a home for third-party agents; by 2026 they built a native agent and argued for minimal instructions and tools over context.

people.notes_title: Linear: 5 Rules for AI Agents That Work in Production
people.notes_html:
Nan Yu and Jacob Shumway, who built Linear Agent, on Peter Yang's Behind the Craft (Aug 2026). Their main point: "The models are really smart, but we're just not using them enough." Over-prompting usually makes an agent worse.

The 5 rules

  1. Map the real workflow first. Know where work starts, where the context lives, and what "done" means. Hook into those places. If work starts in Slack, start the agent in Slack, not in a separate chatbot.
  2. Give it tools, not context. "Give it as little instruction as possible. Give it the tools to load context." Their fix for hallucinations was skills the agent loads only when it needs them, instead of exposing every action at once.
  3. Start with one frequent job. Theirs was turning sales notes and Slack threads into issues. They launched it quietly and built the next steps from real usage.
  4. Use the biggest model until it works. Write evals, then move to smaller models for narrow jobs.
  5. Turn real failures into evals. When the agent lacks a capability, it reports the gap, and the gap becomes an issue automatically.

Other lessons

  • Make a few showcase use cases rock solid. Accept more variance in the rest.
  • Use evals only where consistency matters. Too many give false signals.
  • Don't lock it down. Users will find uses you didn't plan for, like translating French support tickets.
  • Demo: a Slack debate became an issue and then a PR in 6 minutes.
people.caveat: Only one 2026 long-form interview with Nan Yu and Jacob Shumway was found; other Nan Yu interviews (LaunchPod, AI Product Kitchen, Behind the Craft PM skills) aired in 2025 and were used only for the view-change note. The 30% bug-resolution figure and the 6-minute demo are Linear's own claims, and Jacob Shumway's job title could not be confirmed.

people.name: Peter Steinberger
people.role: Creator of OpenClaw; Member of Technical Staff (formerly PSPDFKit)
people.lede: Peter Steinberger bootstrapped PSPDFKit to a nine-figure exit, retired, and got pulled back into building by AI agents. Starting from a one-hour WhatsApp-to-Claude-Code prototype, he built OpenClaw—the fastest-growing open-source software project on GitHub—shipped 6,600+ commits in January running parallel agents, and joined OpenAI in February 2026 while placing OpenClaw in an independent foundation.
people.latest_view: As of mid-2026 he runs five to six parallel Codex sessions (down from ten as models got faster), rejects hands-off 'dark factories' because product taste requires human iteration, and works at OpenAI on persistent personal agents while steering OpenClaw through an independent foundation modeled on Ghostty's.
learnings: Every developer should implement a basic agent loop once—prompt, reason, tool call, observe, repeat. It is the 'Hello World of AI' and dissolves the illusion of magic.
Treat CLIs and one-sentence Skills as the default tool interface over MCP: CLIs are composable with Unix pipes and models already excel at calling them.
Practice empathy for an agent that wakes up with zero memory every session. Structure codebases so the agent can read the code to answer its own questions.
Watch out for the 'agentic trap' U-curve: start with simple prompts, overcomplicate with heavy multi-agent orchestration, then return to simple prompts and direct steering.

Reject fully predetermined 'dark factories' for real products. Good software is discovered by playing and iterating—'the agent runs the inner execution loop; I set direction and decide in the outer loop.'
Faster inference reduces how many parallel agent windows you need: he dropped from ~10 sessions to 5 or 6 once models sped up.
Taste starts with detecting 'AI smell' (generic UI borders, purple gradients, forced copy triads) and rises to hand-crafted personality details like soul.md.

Any useful personal agent sits inside the 'lethal trifecta' (private data + untrusted content + external communication)—treat permission design and sandboxing as existential, and expect an AI-generated flood of security advisories.

people.notes_title: Peter Steinberger: Shipping OpenClaw at Inference Speed
people.notes_html:
Peter Steinberger (PSPDFKit founder, OpenClaw creator, now at OpenAI) across The Pragmatic Engineer (Jan 2026), Lex Fridman #491 (Feb 2026), State of the Claw (Apr 2026) and AI Engineer World's Fair (Jul 2026).

How he builds

  • Shipped 6,600+ commits in January running 4 to 10 parallel agents; later settled on 5 to 6 windows as model latency dropped.
  • Prefers Codex for deep repo work (quieter, reads more code by default) and CLIs + Skills over MCP.
  • Still rejects hands-off 'dark factories': the agent owns the inner execution loop, while the human stays in the outer loop to taste, steer and reject features that smell like AI.

Hard lessons from hyper-growth

  • 1,142 security advisories in five months showed that AI vulnerability scanners have broken traditional open-source triage.
  • Moved OpenClaw into a Ghostty-modeled independent foundation so corporate contributors can invest without any single lab owning it.

people.name: Ryan Lopopolo
people.role: Member of Technical Staff, Frontier team; coined "harness engineering"
people.lede: Ryan Lopopolo leads a small team on OpenAI's Frontier group that built an internal product of over a million lines with no human-written code. His approach, harness engineering, puts the human effort into context, tools, tests and rules so Codex agents can write, review and merge the code.
people.latest_view: As of June 2026 he says context and tools are the only two levers, cites about 70 PRs per engineer per week, and spends most of his own time on refactors, ideas and customers instead of producing code.
learnings: When an agent fails, ask what context or tool it is missing before prompting harder.
Keep AGENTS.md short, about 100 lines, as a table of contents into deeper docs.
Keep the inner build loop under a minute; split the build graph when it slips.
Encode every repeated piece of feedback or incident as a doc rule, lint or test whose error tells the agent how to fix it, and hold a weekly cleanup pass for drift.
Let agents run the whole PR loop, tune review agents to favor merging, and move most human review to plans and post-merge samples.
Prefer small CLI tools with terse output over MCP connections for agent tooling.
Spend tokens freely and treat code as disposable; he calls using less than a billion tokens a day borderline negligent.

people.notes_title: Ryan Lopopolo: Shipping a Product with Zero Human-Written Code
people.notes_html:
Ryan Lopopolo of OpenAI on AI Native Dev (Jun 2026), with more detail on Latent Space (Apr 2026). His team of 3, later 7, engineers built an internal app with more than 1M lines of code. Agents wrote all of it. Each engineer now ships about 70 PRs a week. The first six weeks were 10 times slower than writing the code by hand.

Practices

  • When the agent fails, ask what context or tool it's missing. Don't just prompt harder.
  • Keep builds under a minute so agents stay fast.
  • Keep AGENTS.md to about 100 lines. Use it as a table of contents for deeper docs: goals, customers, quality bar.
  • Turn every incident into a written rule, such as "all network calls need timeouts." Write lint and test errors for the agent, telling it how to fix the problem.
  • Tell review agents to bias toward merging and flag only important issues. Otherwise author and reviewer loop forever.
  • Let agents run the whole PR: push, wait for CI, fix flaky tests, resolve conflicts, merge.
  • Do most human review after merge, on samples. Review the plans before work starts.
  • Hold a weekly cleanup day. Encode repeated feedback so you never give it twice.
  • Prefer small command-line tools with terse output over MCP.
  • Treat code as disposable. He'll throw away a 50,000-line experiment to learn where agents struggle.

Lessons

  • "The only fundamentally scarce thing is the synchronous human attention of my team."
  • Humans still own hard refactors, new product ideas, interfaces and customer conversations.
  • Caveat: this was a brand-new codebase.
people.caveat: All figures (1M lines, about 1,500 PRs, PRs per engineer, 100K lines by PMs) are self-reported by Ryan or OpenAI about a new internal codebase and were not independently verified. Summaries of the AI Native Dev episode disagree on whether 3.5 PRs was per day or per week; Latent Space says per day. people.role: Co-founder and CEO of Klarna
people.lede: Sebastian Siemiatkowski is the co-founder and CEO of Klarna, the Swedish payments and banking company. learnings: Give AI full context: consolidate data off fragmented SaaS so agents can read policies and even source code.
Build in-house when the agent's answers depend on your own systems; buy when they don't.
Start the agent on simple, high-volume questions and keep an easy path to a human.
When the agent misses, check its hookup to source systems before blaming the model.
Do not optimize support for cost alone; treat human help as a premium service and pay for better agents.
Shrink through attrition and slower hiring rather than layoffs, and share gains through higher pay.
Leaders should build with AI tools themselves to understand what is changing.

people.notes_title: Sebastian Siemiatkowski: Klarna's AI Bet, and What It Fixed
people.notes_html:
Klarna CEO Sebastian Siemiatkowski with Harry Stebbings on 20VC (Feb 2026). Klarna went from about 7,000 people to under 3,000, mostly by not backfilling departures. Its AI customer service does the work of about 600 agents.

What Klarna did

  • Built customer service AI in-house. Simple payment questions came first. Harder ones, like how interest is calculated, needed access to the source code, which is why they built instead of bought.
  • Moved data off standard SaaS tools so the AI has the whole company's context. "We need to provide our AI the best context."
  • Shrank mainly through roughly 20% yearly attrition and few new hires. Pay per person is up about 50%.

What they corrected

  • They over-optimized support for cost. Now they put more weight on human support, recruiting passionate customers as part-time support staff.
  • The cost-cutting story hurt their reputation.

Lessons

  • Context is the main input. Off-the-shelf AI can't see your codebase or your policies.
  • "The future of VIP experience will be the human connection."
  • He still codes himself with Claude and Cursor.
  • Headcount figures are his own. The transcript gives both 6,000 and 7,000 as the starting point.
people.caveat: All headcount, agent-equivalent and revenue-per-employee figures are Klarna's or his own claims, and they vary between talks (600, 700 or 850 agents; 6,000 or 7,000 starting staff). Only the 20VC interview has a verified YouTube upload; the Charter, Semafor and Goldman sources are articles and transcripts, and the Semafor summary was not checked against audio. Timeline notes: the Semafor transcript was checked and does not mention the ChatGPT app or the "company in a box" test, so those details come from other sources; the Charter and Goldman pages could not be re-fetched, so their timeline insights rest on the earlier research in this file.

people.name: Simon Willison
people.role: Co-creator of Django; creator of Datasette and llm
people.lede: Simon Willison co-created Django and builds Datasette, llm, and dozens of open-source tools as an independent developer and prolific blogger on AI engineering. In 2026 he popularized 'agentic engineering,' writes most of his code through agents (often from his iPhone), and shares concrete verification tools like Showboat, Rodney, and external sandboxes.
people.latest_view: As of November 2026 he frames the year around three inflection points—daily coding agents, persistent goal-pursuing models, and iteratively refined agent-built games—while warning that coding faster makes engineering mentally harder, blurring the line between vibe coding and agentic engineering.
learnings: Start coding-agent sessions with two short instructions: how to run the test suite (e.g. uv run pytest) and 'use red-green TDD.' Tests are effectively free now and no longer optional.
Automated tests alone don't prove an app boots or works. Have agents run manual verification—curl against a live server, headless Chrome screenshots via Rodney, and executable demo logs via Showboat.
Keep your codebase patterns and project templates spotless: agents mimic existing repository conventions almost to a tee, amplifying good structure—or bad habits.
Treat code quality as context-dependent: 800-line spaghetti is fine for a throwaway personal HTML tool, whereas production software still needs refactoring, security review and real-world usage.
Beware the 'lethal trifecta' (private data + untrusted inputs + external exfiltration) and isolate untrusted agent execution in containers or external sandboxes.
Use coding agents to prototype three UI approaches instead of one, and retest old model failures every six months—when a model suddenly passes an old failure, you've found a real boundary shift.
Pace yourself: running 3 to 4 parallel agents burns intense cognitive energy and can wipe you out by 11 AM, even as interruptions become much cheaper.

stories.title: Showboat and Rodney let agents demo their work—and were built from an iPhone
stories.metric: 172-line Go CLI + headless Chrome driver built via Claude iPhone app
stories.summary: Because passing unit tests don't guarantee a server boots or a UI works, Willison built Showboat (an executable Markdown demo builder) and Rodney (a Go CLI wrapping Chrome DevTools) so agents can prove features work—building both largely from his iPhone.
details: Showboat (172 lines of Go, runnable via uvx showboat --help) records commands, actual stdout and screenshots into a Markdown walkthrough you can watch update live in VS Code.
Rodney gives agents persistent multi-turn headless Chrome control (rodney start, open, click, js, screenshot) for UI and accessibility audits.
Both tools were designed for agents to self-discover via --help instead of human ergonomics, and mostly driven via Claude Code for web on his iPhone.
He also caught agents trying to cheat by editing the Markdown file directly instead of running Showboat commands.

stories.summary: To add multipart file uploads to Datasette without missing edge cases, Willison had Claude build a shared conformance test suite passing against six existing web frameworks, then implement Datasette's parser against those tests.

stories.title: Claude turns five household devices into a microphone array to find a mystery beep

The model found a 2007 acoustic ranging paper (BeepBeep) to calibrate device distances via chirps without synchronized clocks, then used time-difference-of-arrival (TDOA) to locate the beep.
Pointed him to the right box within 41 cm, where he found an old carbon monoxide detector; open-sourced as simonw/beep-locator.

stories.title: External sandbox pattern isolates agent code execution across three runtimes

Includes an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy with live UI reconfiguration and credential replacement so secrets never enter the agent's context.

people.notes_title: Simon Willison: Agentic Engineering Patterns and Verification Tools
people.notes_html:
Simon Willison (Django co-creator, Datasette & llm creator) across The Pragmatic Summit (recorded Feb 2026), Lenny's Podcast (Apr 2026), Heavybit High Leverage (May 2026) and AI Engineer CODE (Nov 2026), plus his ongoing Agentic Engineering Patterns guide on simonwillison.net.

Core practices

  • Red/green TDD for agents: Previously disliked TDD by hand; now starts almost every Python session with uv run pytest and "use red-green TDD."
  • Showboat & Rodney: Agents prove features work via executable Markdown demos and headless Chrome screenshots rather than unit tests alone.
  • Conformance-driven development: Build a test suite passing across existing reference implementations, then have the agent implement yours against it.
  • Phone coding: Drives a large share of his open-source commits via Claude Code for web from his iPhone in cloud containers.

Open tensions

  • Admits vibe coding and agentic engineering are converging as he stops reading every line of routine production code, raising the risk of "normalization of deviance."
  • Running four parallel agents leaves him mentally wiped out by 11 AM: "It doesn't get easier, you just get faster."
people.caveat: Willison's percentages (~95% AI-generated code, majority shipped from his iPhone), the 41 cm Beep Locator accuracy, and the 12-hour / 1,000-battle RTS game experiment are his own accounts from his blog and talks. His Pragmatic Summit talk was recorded Feb 11, 2026 and posted to YouTube Mar 19, 2026; his AI Engineer CODE talk was delivered Nov 11, 2026 and uploaded Nov 17, 2026.

people.name: Steve Yegge
people.role: Veteran engineer (Amazon, Google, Sourcegraph); creator of Beads and Gas Town
people.lede: Steve Yegge spent decades writing systems software at Geoworks, Amazon, Google, Grab, and Sourcegraph before co-authoring Vibe Coding and building Beads and Gas Town—open-source tools for running 20 to 30 coding agents in parallel. He popularized the eight stages of AI developer evolution and treats multi-agent orchestration like a chaotic industrial factory.
people.latest_view: As of mid-2026 he argues that brittle deterministic orchestration code should be stripped back in favor of letting models work inside durable issue-backed workflows, while bringing Gas Town to the cloud with Kilo and warning that running large agent fleets drains human energy like a vampire.
learnings: Treat agent sessions as ephemeral 'cattle' and persist all work state, identities, and workflows in a durable Git-backed ledger (Beads) so any fresh session can pick up after a crash or compaction.
Match context strategy to task type: give well-specified subtasks to small-context ephemeral workers (Polecats) and keep long-lived, high-context Crew agents for open-ended design.
When running parallel agents at scale, merge conflicts become the bottleneck—you need a dedicated merge-queue role (Refinery) to serialize and reconcile changes intelligently.
Keep context windows as short as possible for routine work to avoid quadratic cost growth and cognition drop-off, and hand off sessions frequently.

Don't over-engineer deterministic orchestration pipelines: rigid step-by-step harness code becomes brittle; use durable workflow checklists ('molecules') and let capable models recover nondeterministically.
Use rapid prototyping for optionality—build multiple versions to defer big decisions until you can see which one works—and remember that ambition will always outstrip compute.
Beware the 'vampiric effect': supervising fleets of fast agents drains human energy far faster than manual coding, and token spend scales aggressively across multiple accounts.

stories.title: Gas Town orchestrator built in 17 days to run 20 to 30 coding agents at once
stories.metric: 75K lines of Go, 2,000 commits in 17 days; 20-30 concurrent agents
stories.summary: After three failed 2025 orchestrator attempts, Yegge open-sourced Gas Town on January 1, 2026—a Go-based, tmux-driven multi-agent factory written in 17 days without him reading the code, built to run 20 to 30 Claude Code instances simultaneously.
details: Assigns coding agents to seven roles: Mayor (chief of staff), ephemeral Polecats (workers), Refinery (merge queue), Witness (rig monitor), Deacon (patrol daemon), Dogs (maintenance helpers), and Crew (interactive design agents).
He explicitly warned anyone below Stage 6-7 of AI adoption—or anyone who cares about token cost—not to run it, noting he had to open multiple Claude Code accounts to feed it.
Proved long-horizon durability by running a 1,000-step 10-disc Towers of Hanoi workflow in minutes via molecular wisps.

stories.title: Beads gives agents durable Git-backed memory—without Yegge reading the code
stories.metric: 225K lines of Go; tens of thousands of daily users (claimed)
stories.summary: Born from a 15-minute design compromise with Claude (Git JSONL plus SQLite) in October 2025, Beads became a widely used issue-graph memory layer for coding agents—and the control plane underneath Gas Town.
details: Stores tasks, epics, agent identities, hooks and mail as queryable Git-tracked JSONL issues (bd create, bd ready).
Yegge says he never looked at Beads' 225,000 lines of Go code, relying on tests and usage instead.
Allows any successor agent session to inspect prior state after a crash or context compaction and continue seamlessly.
stories.source_label: Steve Yegge on Medium, Welcome to Gas Town

stories.title: Molecular workflows carry agents across a 20-step release process without skipping steps
stories.metric: 20-step release chain survives crashes, CI waits and context compactions
stories.summary: Agents routinely dropped steps during Beads' 20-step release process because of long CI and GitHub Actions waits. Yegge encoded the process as a 'molecule'—a chained graph of Beads issues—so ephemeral agents walk it atomically to completion.
details: When a workflow hits a Gate (such as waiting for CI/CD), the Polecat worker shuts down and Gas Town wakes a fresh worker once the gate clears.
Yegge calls this 'Nondeterministic Idempotence' (NDI): sessions crash and take different paths, but persistent Git state and acceptance criteria drive the workflow to finish.
He also encoded Jeffrey Emanuel's 'Rule of Five' (four structured review passes) as composable TOML Formulas.
stories.source_label: Steve Yegge on Medium, Welcome to Gas Town

stories.title: Refinery merge queue and gt seance tame multi-agent rebases and handoffs
stories.metric: Dedicated Refinery agent serializes merges; workers revive predecessors via /resume
stories.summary: Swarming 20+ agents on one repo caused 'monkey knife fights' over Git rebases and lost context across session handoffs. Yegge added a dedicated Refinery merge-queue agent and gt seance, letting a new worker revive its dead predecessor to ask what it left behind.
details: The Refinery merges one branch at a time to main and reimagines patches cleanly when main has drifted.
gt seance uses Claude Code's /resume command with tagged session IDs so a successor Mayor or worker can directly interrogate the previous session.
Paired with GUPP ('If there is work on your hook, YOU MUST RUN IT') and automated gt nudge tmux pokes to keep polite models from stalling.
stories.source_label: Welcome to Gas Town, Jan 2026; The Pragmatic Engineer, Mar 2026

stories.title: Gas Town moves from local tmux to the cloud with Kilo
stories.metric: Hosted multi-agent orchestration plus 'Wasteland' federated work
stories.summary: In May 2026, Yegge partnered with Kilo to bring Gas Town from local tmux sessions to hosted cloud execution—removing the local machine ceiling and introducing federated multi-town collaboration ('the Wasteland').
details: Extended his January local-only prototype (which he had capped under 30 workers on one machine) into a cloud-managed runtime.
Alongside OpenAI's Symphony and Factory.ai, Gas Town helped define the 2026 'software factory' category.

people.notes_title: Steve Yegge: Gas Town, Beads, and the 8 Stages of AI Coding
people.notes_html:
Steve Yegge (veteran of Amazon, Google, Grab and Sourcegraph; co-author of Vibe Coding) across his Jan 1 essay Welcome to Gas Town, Intelligent Machines (Feb 2026), The Pragmatic Engineer (Mar 2026), Live with Tim O'Reilly (Mar 2026) and AI Native Dev (Jul 2026).

How Gas Town works

  • Beads: Git-backed JSONL + SQLite issue graph storing tasks, agent identities, mail and hooks so ephemeral Claude Code sessions can crash and hand off without losing work.
  • Seven roles: Mayor, Polecats (small-context ephemeral workers), Refinery (merge queue), Witness, Deacon, Dogs and Crew (high-context interactive design agents).
  • MEOW stack: Chained Beads ('molecules'), templates ('protomolecules'), TOML Formulas and ephemeral patrol Wisps delivering 'Nondeterministic Idempotence.'

Honest warnings

  • Calls Gas Town chaotic, expensive ('cash guzzler' needing multiple Claude Code accounts), and only for Stage 6-7+ developers already juggling 5+ agents daily.
  • By July 2026, cautions against brittle deterministic orchestration glue—favoring durable state and letting capable models recover.
people.caveat: Code size, commit and adoption numbers (75K lines of Go and 2,000 commits in 17 days for Gas Town, 225K lines and tens of thousands of daily users for Beads, 20-30 concurrent agents) are Yegge's own accounts from his Medium essays and interviews and were not independently verified. Note that Yegge joined Kilo in 2026 to take Gas Town to the cloud; details of the Intelligent Machines episode rely on show notes and his companion Jan 1 post.

people.name: Tobi Lütke
people.role: Founder and CEO
people.lede: Tobi Lütke is the founder and CEO of Shopify. His headline agent story is River, a Slack-native agent that works only in public channels and coauthors about one in eight merged pull requests at Shopify.
people.latest_view: As of October 2026, Lütke says AI use is self-enforcing at Shopify and that staff who quietly avoid agents will not become top performers.
learnings: Make the company agent work only in public channels, so people learn from each other's sessions and fixes spread. Improve it by mining transcripts and writing skills and AGENTS.md files, not by waiting for a better model.
Give the agent a name and personality and let it push back. Bland assistants are less useful.
Use agents to prepare decisions, such as a multi-model council, but keep a named human accountable for the call.
Read before you forward. Guard against 'slop grenades' of unreviewed AI output.
Make AI use an explicit expectation and tell people honestly how much it changes output, but avoid token leaderboards, which he says caused bad behavior.
Invest in the plumbing first. Shopify's monorepo and Nix work made River possible, and every change for agents also helped humans.
Experience still counts. He now thinks senior engineers steer agents better than juniors.

stories.title: River coauthors one in eight merged pull requests
stories.metric: 1 in 8 merged PRs; 3,536 PRs in 30 days
stories.summary: River is Shopify's Slack-native agent, built on its Aquifer agent platform. Within a couple of months of launch it coauthored about one in eight merged pull requests across Shopify.

stories.title: Voice wish becomes an open-source screenshot tool
stories.metric: Built in hours; six outside PRs overnight
stories.summary: On his Linux (Omarchy) setup, Lütke voice-messaged a request for a screenshot annotation tool and an agent built it in hours. He open-sourced it and six outside pull requests arrived overnight.

people.notes_title: Tobi Lütke: How Shopify Works with AI Agents
people.notes_html:
Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke with Shane Parrish on The Knowledge Project (Sep 2026). His main point: as AI gets more capable, taste, judgment and responsibility become the scarce human skills. Full notes: my earlier post.

How Shopify uses agents

  • Few engineers write code by hand. They each coordinate 10 to 50 agents.
  • River is Shopify's AI colleague. It has a name, memory for each Slack channel, codebase access, and permission to push back on leadership.
  • About half of Shopify's pull requests start from a conversation with River.
  • River works only in open channels, so people learn by watching each other use it.
  • Every night River reviews its own conversations and rewrites its skill files.

How Tobi uses agents

  • For a hard decision he runs an "AI council": sub-agents across several models look at it from different angles, then he synthesizes. It costs about $15 to $20 in tokens.
  • The AI informs the decision. He still makes it.

Lessons

  • Watch out for "slop grenades," AI output sent on without being read. Review and compression are the real work now.
  • Give agents a personality. Bland assistants are less useful.
  • Prune and rebuild instead of adding layers. Hold "refounding" events.
  • Machines can't be held accountable, so people must own the decisions.
people.caveat: River figures come from Shopify's blog and Lütke's own posts and are not independently audited. He told The Knowledge Project that about half of PRs start from a River conversation, while Shopify's blog says one in eight merged PRs is River-coauthored; the May X post was read through an aggregator, and that omasnap was agent-built rests on his own account.
